newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to send U.S. negotiator to Middle East.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to send U.S. negotiator to Middle East.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has asked U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross to return to the Middle East for talks with Israeli and Palestinian leaders, the White House announced late on Tuesday.
The announcement comes in the wake of last Friday's suicide bombing at a cafe in Tel Aviv, which put serious new strain on peace talks between Israel and Palestinians.
"The president has asked Ambassador Dennis Ross to travel to the Middle East tomorrow for consultations on the peace process," said White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn.
Glynn said Ross would meet with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"It is expected that Ambassador Ross will be back by next weekend to brief the president and Secretary Albright," she said.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright contacted Arafat by telephone in Bangladesh on Tuesday and talked him into returning to the Mideast for talks, CNN reported.

The announcement was a glimmer of good news as Israeli troops clashed with Palestinians on Tuesday for the sixth consecutive day over construction of a Jewish settlement at Jabel Abu Ghneim (Har Homa in Hebrew) launched on March 18.

Relations between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation have been overtaken by violence and mutual accusations a week after bulldozers began ploughing a hill in Arab East Jerusalem to ready the area for construction.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the PLO of directing the violence, while Palestinian officials said the Israeli leader was responsible for the unrest.
Last Friday, a Palestinian suicide bomber killed three Israeli women at a cafe in Tel Aviv.
Netanyahu and Arafat have not ruled out a crisis summit, but each side had laid down markers for possible talks.
Ross has been focused on trying to get Israel and the Palestinian Authority back into a meaningful dialogue.

As part of a campaign to shore up the embattled peace process, Ross, in a recent television interview, underscored the need "for 100 percent effort" in fighting terrorism and said "e'd like to see them (Palestinians) do more."
U.S. officials said for some time they have been concerned Arafat had softened a crackdown that left two Islamic extrmist groups, Hamas and Islamic Jihad, nearly broken.
Palestinians deny charges by Netanyahu that Arafat has given Islamic militants a tacit "green light" to carry out attacks including Friday's bombing.
In other efforts to keep the Mideast peace process alive, the United States on Monday also rescheduled a Washington visit for Jordan's King Hussein.
